articles.title: Taylor Swift’s Audience Is Growing Up. Her Music Is Devolving.
articles.text: Some music pulls you out of yourself, jolting you with the recognition that the person who’s singing is just as complex as you are. Some music gets you to surrender to the fact that you’re merely an overgrown baby who responds to repetition and rhyme. And some music strands you in a state of embarrassment at the human condition. Taylor Swift has lately been making music in that last category, and the discomfort is reaching terminal levels. On Friday, she released four new tracks for The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore , the deluxe edition of her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl . Bonus tracks are usually thought of as, well, bonuses—treats for the fans and incidental to an artist’s arc. But the reaction this time has drawn so much disgust that it’s like Swift mailed a horse’s head to each of her listeners. Swift has long led a cultural turn toward revaluing feelings and sounds that were once thought of as childish—but now her audience seems restless to grow up. Produced by the factory-precise hitmakers Max Martin and Shellback, Showgirl was billed as her return to pure pop after an experimental detour on 2024’s The Tortured Poets Department . Showgirl enjoyed the best-selling first week in music history—not because it amazed the broadest audience possible but because it goaded superfans to buy multiple copies . Some of those fans began to grumble that their idol was taking them for granted. Showgirl ’s music mostly felt like a bad sitcom: brightly toned but cynically spirited, verbose but charmless. When Swift announced deluxe tracks last week after posting a photo of herself in an austere cocktail dress, it seemed possible she’d taken the public feedback and refined Showgirl ’s fluffy, empty aesthetic. Alas, no. Encore does contain some intriguing ideas: strings on “Patient Zero” that sound like they’re playing from the walls of Enya’s castle, a sensitive and somewhat mysterious character study on “Babylon.” But, as on the original Showgirl , the music is too stiff to soar. Verses evoke “Baby Shark” with blocky melodies that overly emphasize each rhyming syllable. Her lyrics, usually laden with double and triple meanings, invite little extended analysis. Sometimes she raps like a funky uncle delivering a wedding toast. The worst offender is “Cleveland!” Pattering like a musical-theater sidekick, she complains about haters who make fun of her dancing and her looks, until the chorus announces that everything’s fine because her man loves her. Perky piano and glockenspiel imitate ecstatic classics such as Commodores’ “Easy” and Sufjan Stevens’s “Chicago” in the same way that stick figures imitate human beings. The problem isn’t that she sounds happy, and neither is it that she’s nah-nah-nah ing at critics for the zillionth time in her career. It’s that the song hits the same note (literally, figuratively, lyrically, musically) over and over. Listening feels like getting beaten with a candy cane. Swift’s stans are notorious for their loyalty, but online, the consensus around Encore is harsh. “I’m a Swiftie and Even I Think These New Songs Are Terrible,” the headline of Poppie Platt’s review in The Telegraph reads. The superfan-slash- critic who goes by the name Swiftologist recorded a reaction in which his voice cracked as he said, “It’s so hard to be the Swiftologist at a time like this!” One strain of backlash has centered on the notion that she’s too old to be making music this simplistic . On X, someone posted her lyrics with a picture of Sex and the City ’s Samantha saying, “If you were 25, that would be adorable, but you’re 32, so that’s just stupid.” Swift will turn 37 in December. This line of critique is a little surprising given how Swift has long subverted expectations about her age and gender. As a teenager, she wrote songs that weren’t so much wise beyond her years as reflective of the truth that young people have brains and use them. “Fifteen,” released when she was 18, empathized with and advised girls just a few years younger than her; on “22,” she both celebrated and mocked her own 22-year-old giddiness. In titling her hit 2014 album 1989 , after her birth year, she practically insisted that she be seen as the consummate Millennial. As she got older, her anxieties as a 30-something in a field that loves to discard older women became a source of inspiration: She sang on 2022’s “Anti-Hero” that she felt like a “monster on a hill” next to the “sexy baby” singers coming up behind her. Her music itself has suggested a deep rethinking of what it means to mature. Reconciling complex storytelling and catchy melodies in fresh and clever ways with each release , Swift has conveyed that growing older needn’t mean ditching the pleasures inherent to pop. Neither does it mean discarding the vulnerability, the self-interest, and the swooning that are typically seen as teenager fare. This proved influential at a time when childhood and adulthood were colliding in so many corners of culture—with shorts at the office , comic-book movies at the Oscars, and stuffed animals on adult backpacks . In the 21st century, pop culture doesn’t ask grown-ups to put away childish things; it urges them to upgrade them, remix them, and vest them with new importance to suit each phase of life. [ Read: How did Taylor Swift convince the world that she’s relatable? ] But lately the civilizationally ominous problems with clinging to youth are starting to seem glaring. Surgery and skin care in the pursuit of dewiness are warping people’s relationship with their own face . America’s romance recession has the air of a cooties panic. Democracy has been destabilized by the schoolyard-bully stylings of Donald Trump and his propagandists posting anime from official White House accounts. Last year, the musician Patrick Cosmos proposed a “new unified theory of American reality” called “everyone is twelve now.” The theory went viral because it really did seem to explain such disparate phenomena as Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s meaty diet and Emerald Fennell’s slimy, silly Wuthering Heights . At some point, a cultural countermovement calling back to earlier ideals of adulthood—restraint, nuance, care for the collective—seems likely to catch on. In music, that turn may be under way already. The breakout soul singer Olivia Dean, at age 27, projects the calm sophistication of last century’s torch singers. The country star Ella Langley just smashed the record for the longest-running Hot 100 No. 1 with music that emanates seen-it-all, world-weary wisdom (she’s also 27). In August, at Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival, a class of singers that’s been tagged as “girly pop” organized a serious-minded and historically informed effort for abortion rights and women’s health. Even music’s recent confrontation over Israel and Palestine resembles a coming-of-age crisis: Ed Sheeran claimed that he avoided commenting on politics in deference to kids in his audience, but eventually, the pressure to speak was so great that he took a stand. Maybe it’s wishful thinking to glean a trend from those examples, but the simple truth is that time imparts lessons even to those who seem to resist aging. At the MTV VMAs on Sunday, where Swift debuted her “Patient Zero” video (a pulpy romantic-horror clip starring Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson), many accolades went to another icon who’s navigated the seasons of life in her own way: Madonna. Although the 68-year-old singer’s commitment to singing about sex and dancing in corsets leads many critics to hold her up as a sad example of not acting one’s age, really she’s shown how an aversion to compromise can keep a career viable over decades. In 1998, at age 39, she released Ray of Light , an album that saw her evolve her lyrical purview—to matters of the soul and society—as she pushed her sound in lush, yet still clubby, directions. This year, she put out Confessions II , a fan-adored album of dance bangers that also managed to deliver a forthright statement about memory and mortality. Swift’s fans, meanwhile, are exchanging theories for why she’s gone Benjamin Button . One popular (but dubious) explanation is that after marrying Travis Kelce, she’s too happy to make interesting music. Another is that everything she’s doing is “satire” (okay, but is it good?). But maybe Swift just made a strategic call after noticing how jejune pop culture has become—and in doing so, underestimated her audience. Undying support for a pop star is a fundamentally childish behavior, and although Swift’s audience still craves her brand of bubblegum confessionalism, they also expect at least the level of sophistication that she’s shown before. And at a time when so much else is regressing, artists’ role is to show us what moving forward might look like.

articles.title: Lịch thi đấu Asiad ngày 30/9: Boxing chắc huy chương, chờ judo và vật bứt phá
articles.text:
TPO - Hai võ sĩ boxing Nguyễn Thị Tâm và Lưu Diễm Quỳnh đã chắc chắn có huy chương, nhưng vẫn phải vượt những đối thủ mạnh ở bán kết để giành vé vào chung kết. Judo nữ và vật tự do nữ 68kg cũng mở ra cơ hội bổ sung huy chương cho thể thao Việt Nam trong ngày 30/9.
Tâm điểm là hai trận bán kết boxing, lần lượt diễn ra lúc 11h15 và 12h. Nguyễn Thị Tâm, hạng 51kg, gặp Alua Balkibekova của Kazakhstan, võ sĩ từng hai lần vô địch thế giới và hai lần vô địch châu Á. Ở hạng 75kg, Lưu Diễm Quỳnh đối đầu Bao Ziyi của Trung Quốc, tay đấm 20 tuổi từng giành HCĐ giải vô địch trẻ thế giới.
Trước đó, Tâm và Quỳnh giành quyền vào bán kết sau những chiến thắng 5-0 ở tứ kết. Theo thể thức giải, các võ sĩ vào bán kết đều chắc chắn có huy chương. Nếu thắng tiếp, hai tuyển thủ Việt Nam sẽ giành quyền tranh HCV.
Judo có hai võ sĩ tranh tài ở hạng 48kg và 52kg. Hà Ngọc Chi gặp đối thủ Ấn Độ, còn Lâm Thị Ngân Hà chạm trán võ sĩ Nepal ở vòng loại lúc 9h. Các trận bán kết dự kiến từ 11h20; hai trận chung kết lần lượt diễn ra lúc 15h20 và 16h20.
Đây là cơ hội tranh huy chương trực tiếp, dù thử thách không nhỏ bởi judo Việt Nam chỉ có hai tuyển thủ dự Asiad 20 và cả Chi lẫn Ngân Hà đều chưa thể giành huy chương ở giải vô địch châu Á hồi tháng 4.
Vật cũng khởi tranh trong ngày 30/9. Đặng Thị Linh thi đấu hạng 68kg nữ từ 8h30, với các vòng loại, bán kết và đấu vớt trước loạt tranh huy chương lúc 16h. Ban huấn luyện đặt mục tiêu HCĐ cho đội tuyển vật, đồng thời xác định các đô vật nữ là nhóm có khả năng tiệm cận thành tích này.
Linh từng vào tứ kết hạng 76kg tại Asiad 19, nhưng lần này cô sẽ thi đấu ở hạng cân 68kg. Vòng loại và các trận tranh huy chương của hạng cân này diễn ra trong cùng một ngày.
Các môn khác chủ yếu bước vào vòng khởi đầu. Sau khi nội dung đôi nữ giành tấm HCV thứ hai cho Đoàn Thể thao Việt Nam ngày 29/9, cầu mây tiếp tục là kỳ vọng vàng. Theo đó, cầu mây 4 nam gặp Myanmar, còn đội nữ gặp Ấn Độ từ 7h.
Bắn súng có Phạm Quang Huy, Lại Công Minh và Nguyễn Đình Thành thi đấu vòng loại 25m súng ngắn bắn nhanh lúc 7h40. Quang Huy từng giành HCV Asiad 19 ở nội dung 10m súng ngắn hơi.
Golf bắt đầu vòng 1 từ 4h30, với ba golfer nam Nguyễn Anh Minh, Lê Khánh Hưng, Nguyễn Tuấn Anh và hai golfer nữ Lê Nguyễn Minh Anh, Nguyễn Khánh Linh.
TPO - Năm golfer Việt Nam bước vào tranh tài tại Asiad 20 từ ngày 30/9, đối đầu nhiều đối thủ giàu kinh nghiệm trên sân Kasugai Country Club, Nhật Bản. Đây cũng là cơ hội để các tuyển thủ trẻ tích lũy trải nghiệm ở đấu trường lớn của châu lục.
TPO - Sau chiến thắng 2-0 trước đội tuyển Việt Nam, đội trưởng đội tuyển quốc gia Thái Lan, Chanathip Songkrasin, đã có những chia sẻ thẳng thắn và giàu cảm xúc về màn so tài đỉnh cao này.
TPO - Sự sắc bén của Anthony Gordon và Harry Kane cùng tấm thẻ đỏ của đội chủ nhà đã giúp tuyển Anh vượt qua CH Séc 2-0 ngay tại Prague, qua đó có chiến thắng đầu tiên tại UEFA Nations League
TPO - Lamine Yamal tiếp tục trở thành tâm điểm trong chiến thắng tưng bừng của Tây Ban Nha trước Croatia. Màn trình diễn chói sáng của tài năng trẻ 19 tuổi giúp La Roja giành thắng lợi 4-1, đồng thời nối dài chuỗi trận bất bại đầy ấn tượng.
TPO - Nhận định bóng đá U23 Trung Quốc vs U23 Hàn Quốc, Asiad 20 - Thông tin lực lượng, đội hình dự kiến, phong độ, lịch sử đối đầu. U23 Trung Quốc vs U23 Hàn Quốc đem đến những phong cách trái ngược, với một bên tấn công bùng nổ còn bên kia lấy phòng ngự làm triết lý vận hành.
TPO - Trận thua 0-2 trước Thái Lan vào tối 29/9 vừa khoét sâu thêm một nỗi buồn cái dớp sân trung lập của đội tuyển Việt Nam. Suốt chiều dài lịch sử bóng đá khu vực, đội tuyển Việt Nam từng đánh sập "thánh địa" Rajamangala, nhưng đội dường như vẫn chưa thể tìm ra lời giải khi đấu người Thái trên sân trung lập.
TPO - Trận thua 0-2 trước Thái Lan tại bảng B - FIFA ASEAN Cup 2026 không chỉ khiến đội tuyển Việt Nam mất vé vào chung kết, mà còn đẩy thầy trò HLV Kim Sang-sik xuống sát ranh giới báo động trên bảng xếp hạng FIFA. Liệu vị trí trong Top 100 thế giới của Các chiến binh Sao Vàng có bị đe dọa?
TPO - Chiến thắng thuyết phục 2-0 trước đại kình địch Việt Nam vào tối 29/9 đã châm ngòi cho một làn sóng cuồng nhiệt bùng nổ khắp các nền tảng mạng xã hội xứ Chùa vàng.
TPO - Trang chủ Liên đoàn Bóng đá châu Á gọi bàn thắng mở tỷ số của Sarach là pha sút xa tuyệt vời. Trong khi đó, Việt Nam tạo ra nhiều cơ hội nhưng không tận dụng được.
TPO - Thất bại 0-2 trước Thái Lan tại FIFA ASEAN Cup 2026 trở thành tâm điểm chú ý của truyền thông Indonesia, trong đó CNN Indonesia cho rằng sự vắng mặt của Nguyễn Xuân Son khiến đội bóng của HLV Kim Sang-sik thiếu những phương án gây đột biến trước hàng thủ chơi kín kẽ của người Thái.
TPO - HLV Anthony Hudson và các học trò hoàn thành mục tiêu giành chiến thắng trước Việt Nam. Ông bước vào phòng họp báo trong tâm thế hứng khởi của người chiến thắng.
TPO - HLV Kim Sang-sik tiếc nuối khi Việt Nam không thể ghi bàn vào lưới Thái Lan. Ông gửi lời xin lỗi CĐV Việt Nam vì không giành vé vào chung kết FIFA ASEAN Cup 2026.
TPO - Sau khi Tạ Ngọc Tưởng đưa đội lên vị trí thứ hai, sự cố rơi gậy ở chặng kế tiếp khiến đội tiếp sức 4x400m nam Việt Nam đánh mất cơ hội cạnh tranh huy chương và cán đích cuối cùng với thành tích 3 phút 35 giây 71.
Ca sĩ Hà Lê sẽ tham gia Run For The Heart 2026, giải chạy dự kiến tổ chức ngày 6/12 tại công viên Yên Sở. Anh cho biết muốn góp sức lan tỏa chương trình và hỗ trợ trẻ em mắc bệnh tim có hoàn cảnh khó khăn.
Trước ngày tranh tài tại Nhật Bản, đội tuyển golf Việt Nam nhận được sự đồng hành của Anfarm. Sự tiếp sức này có ý nghĩa lớn trong bối cảnh đội dự Asiad 20 bằng nguồn kinh phí xã hội hóa, trong đó có những gia đình phải tự lo một phần chi phí.

articles.title: Điểm mở dải phân cách trên QL1 qua Hà Tĩnh tạo giao cắt nguy hiểm, tiềm ẩn nguy cơ tai nạn
articles.text:
Những cú cắt ngang dòng xe
Trên quốc lộ 1 qua Hà Tĩnh, không khó để bắt gặp những tình huống phương tiện chuyển hướng đột ngột tại các điểm mở dải phân cách. Xe máy, xe đạp điện, thậm chí ô tô có lúc tạt ngang dòng phương tiện, chuyển hướng mà không bật tín hiệu xin đường hoặc không giảm tốc độ.
Có trường hợp phương tiện còn đi ngược chiều để nhanh chóng tiếp cận điểm mở thay vì di chuyển đến vị trí quay đầu đúng quy định. Khi dòng xe trên quốc lộ 1 vẫn liên tục lưu thông, những hành vi này tạo ra các điểm xung đột mà chỉ cần một bên thiếu quan sát hoặc xử lý chậm có thể dẫn tới va chạm.
Trong điều kiện mưa lớn, sương mù hoặc thời tiết bất lợi, tầm nhìn bị hạn chế, việc quan sát dòng xe đối diện càng khó khăn. Nếu phương tiện vẫn giữ tốc độ cao khi tiếp cận điểm giao cắt, nguy cơ xảy ra sự cố càng tăng.
Đơn cử, vào khoảng 13h05 ngày 11/9, tại Km549+150 quốc lộ 1, xảy ra vụ tai nạn giữa xe ô tô bán tải và xe máy khiến một người tử vong.
Thời điểm trên, xe bán tải do tài xế H.V.D (SN 1995, trú xã Thạch Khê, Hà Tĩnh) điều khiển theo hướng Nam - Bắc. Khi đến khu vực điểm mở dải phân cách, ô tô va chạm với xe máy do ông N.T.B (SN 1971, trú xã Kỳ Anh) điều khiển theo chiều ngược lại, đang qua điểm mở.
Nguyên nhân vụ tai nạn đang được cơ quan chức năng điều tra, làm rõ.
Theo nhận định ban đầu của lực lượng CSGT Hà Tĩnh, vụ việc có liên quan đến việc người điều khiển xe máy khi qua điểm mở không chú ý quan sát, không nhường đường; trong khi tài xế ô tô bán tải cũng không chú ý quan sát, không chấp hành hiệu lệnh của hệ thống biển báo và không giảm tốc độ khi qua khu vực giao nhau.
Không để điểm mở thành điểm xung đột
Trước những nguy cơ trên, việc rà soát, đánh giá lại các điểm mở đang được cơ quan chức năng Hà Tĩnh và đơn vị quản lý đường bộ triển khai.
Trung tá Lê Doãn Thái, Phó trưởng phòng CSGT Công an tỉnh Hà Tĩnh, cho biết: Thời gian qua, lực lượng CSGT tăng cường tuyên truyền, hướng dẫn người dân chú ý quan sát khi lưu thông qua các điểm mở dải phân cách; đồng thời tăng cường tuần tra, kiểm soát và xử lý các trường hợp vi phạm.
Lực lượng CSGT cũng phối hợp với công an các địa phương và cơ quan quản lý đường bộ rà soát hệ thống điểm mở, đánh giá những vị trí bất hợp lý, tiềm ẩn nguy cơ mất an toàn hoặc không còn phù hợp với thực tế để có phương án xử lý.
Theo đó, những điểm mở không cần thiết hoặc tiềm ẩn nguy cơ cao có thể được đóng; những vị trí cần duy trì phải được nghiên cứu điều chỉnh phù hợp, đồng thời bổ sung biển báo, sơn vạch kẻ đường, gờ giảm tốc và các giải pháp tổ chức giao thông cần thiết.
Ông Trần Thế Thành, Phó trưởng Văn phòng Quản lý đường bộ II.3 (Khu Quản lý đường bộ II - Cục Đường bộ Việt Nam), cho biết: Trên cơ sở kiến nghị của địa phương, đơn vị đã phối hợp với các cơ quan chức năng đóng 3 điểm mở dải phân cách trên quốc lộ 1 qua các xã Kỳ Xuân, Cẩm Xuyên.
Theo ông Thành, hiện các đơn vị tiếp tục rà soát những điểm mở còn lại để triển khai biện pháp bảo đảm an toàn giao thông. Một số điểm mở cũng được rào chắn để ngăn phương tiện qua lại, chỉ dành lối cho người đi bộ.

articles.title: Cháy căn hộ tầng 11 chung cư ở TPHCM
articles.text:
TPO - Một căn hộ ở tầng 11 chung cư Conic Boulevard (xã Tân Nhựt, TPHCM) bốc cháy tối 29/9. Chuông báo cháy vang lên, nhiều cư dân di chuyển bằng cầu thang bộ ra khu vực an toàn.
Clip vụ cháy chung cư ở TPHCM.
Theo thông tin ban đầu, khoảng 18h30 ngày 29/9, đám cháy bùng phát bên trong một căn hộ tại tầng 11, block B chung cư Conic Boulevard trên đường Huỳnh Bá Chánh, xã Tân Nhựt. Khói đen từ căn hộ lan ra khu vực ban công.
Cùng thời điểm, hệ thống chuông báo cháy của tòa nhà vang lên. Cư dân tại các tầng thông báo cho nhau, sử dụng cầu thang bộ để xuống khu vực an toàn.
Hình ảnh khói đen thoát ra từ căn hộ chung cư.
Nhận tin báo, lực lượng chức năng đến hiện trường, phối hợp bảo vệ tòa nhà và đội PCCC cơ sở triển khai chữa cháy, hỗ trợ người dân thoát hiểm và điều tiết giao thông khu vực.
Đám cháy sau đó cơ bản được khống chế. Theo thông tin ban đầu, vụ việc không gây thiệt hại về người. Cơ quan chức năng đang xác minh nguyên nhân vụ cháy và thống kê thiệt hại tài sản.
TPO - Hai vụ tai nạn liên tiếp trong 10 ngày khiến thầy dạy lái xe tử vong đã bộc lộ rõ rủi ro từ xe tập lái trên cao tốc. Việc giáo viên đưa học viên thiếu kỹ năng thực hành tại các tuyến đường này đang đe dọa trực tiếp an toàn giao thông và đặt ra dấu hỏi về quy trình đào tạo lái xe thực tế.

Ông yêu cầu báo cáo tiến độ hằng ngày và làm rõ trách nhiệm của chủ đầu tư khi công trình mới đạt khoảng 80% khối lượng.

articles.title: Trump’s Latest Appeal to Russia Could Outrage Even His Allies
articles.text: A few months ago, Donald Trump’s envoy to Eastern Europe came to the president with a new idea for breaking the deadlock in U.S. relations with Moscow. The plan involved a quid pro quo reminiscent of the Cold War: The Kremlin would free some political prisoners, and the United States would reward their release by easing sanctions on the Russian economy. Trump signed on. This new initiative, which is still in its early stages and has not been previously reported, promises to advance several of Trump’s goals at once. It would help reintegrate Russia into the global economy and broaden Trump’s talks with the Kremlin beyond the intractable war in Ukraine, which his envoys have failed to end after more than a year of diplomacy. It would create a path for the U.S. to sign lucrative deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals, and other commodities. As a bonus, the release of prisoners on humanitarian grounds could bolster Trump’s case for his long-coveted Nobel Peace Prize. This fresh approach to dealing with the Kremlin, however, is likely to outrage the Ukrainians, the Europeans, and even many of Trump’s allies on Capitol Hill. Any potential business deal between the U.S. and Russia would risk funneling money to the Russian military even as it continues to terrorize Ukraine and threatens a wider war against U.S. allies in Europe. Earlier this month, Trump signed a law co-authored by Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator, authorizing Trump to impose severe sanctions on Russia and its trading partners. Even against that backdrop, Trump’s diplomatic envoys have been quietly looking for ways to ease U.S. sanctions and do business with Moscow. John Coale, the envoy who proposed the new strategy involving the release of political prisoners, has spent more than a year testing it in Belarus, Russia’s closest ally. In talks with that country’s dictator, Alexander Lukashenko, Coale won the release of hundreds of prisoners from Belarusian jails. In exchange, the U.S. has eased its sanctions on Lukashenko’s regime and pursued a deal to buy his country’s most valuable export, a type of fertilizer known as potash. With Trump’s blessing, Coale has now set out to try the same trick with Vladimir Putin in Russia. Last week, Trump announced that the U.S. is negotiating a “massive” potash deal with Belarus. Coale, a former lawyer to Trump, told me that Russia is also a part of those negotiations. Since the start of the war in Ukraine, the U.S. has avoided trade deals involving Russia. This one would mark a rare exception if finalized. In Coale’s view, it would also help advance the cause of peace. “All this stuff works toward the possibility of peace,” Coale told me. “The more interaction, the more trade-offs—either economic, prisoners, or whatever—leads step by step toward, hopefully, peace. That’s kind of the mission.” The Ukrainians see it differently. Belarus has served as a Russian staging ground for the invasion of Ukraine, and Lukashenko has provided the Russian military with bases, supplies, and ammunition. During his visit to New York last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told me he would try his best to “block” any attempt to lift the sanctions on Russia before the war ends. “But it’s difficult,” he conceded. The Russian economy is roughly 10 times larger than Ukraine’s. “It’s very difficult to compare with Russian money, with their business.” E ver since Putin first sent troops into Ukraine, in 2014, the U.S. and Europe have used just about every variety of sanction to punish Russia for its attacks, targeting Moscow’s political elites, its industrial base, its banking system, its energy sector, and other sources of money and technology that Putin needs to wage the war. Trump temporarily eased some of those sanctions this spring, when he allowed Russia to sell more fuel on the global market, hoping to alleviate the oil-price shock caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Ukraine denounced that decision at the time. In his speech last week to the United Nations General Assembly, Zelensky again urged the West to intensify and enforce its sanctions on Russia, including the new measures Trump signed into law this month. “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time,” he said. In reference to Putin, he added: “Limit his money. Limit his war.” [ Read: The abandonment of Ukraine ] But the American negotiators have taken a softer approach, seeking to pacify Putin with the promise of economic growth. After his visit to the Kremlin earlier this month, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner described the money to be made on the back of a peace deal. He told the audience at a conference in Kyiv that business deals—or, as he called them, “prosperity agreements”—form an essential part of Trump’s strategy. If they agree to a cease-fire, Putin and Zelensky “need to have something to look forward to” in terms of foreign investment and higher living standards for their citizens. “I think that’s what gets the societies invested and excited about peace,” Kushner said via video link at the Yalta European Strategy conference. “Also it becomes, in some ways, your best security guarantee.” Ukrainians, of course, have plenty of reasons to be excited about peace apart from the prospect of higher wages. The casualty count in this war has topped 2 million people, killed and wounded, on both sides, and Russia continues to bombard Ukrainian cities day and night. Ukraine has responded with a campaign of strikes against various targets in Russia, particularly its oil refineries and other energy infrastructure. As part of any peace deal, Zelensky has demanded ironclad security guarantees from his Western allies to ensure that Russia does not attack again in the future. His negotiators told me that they do not see “prosperity agreements” with Russia as any kind of security guarantee for Ukraine. Quite the opposite: They see Western trade with Russia as a way for Putin to strengthen his military and continue the war. In recent weeks, Ukrainians have been dismayed to hear Trump’s envoys use peace negotiations as a means of advancing business deals. “This is the thing that drives them now,” one of the negotiators told me of the Americans. A second negotiator added: “They believe in the magic of business. They think that if they make these business deals, the Russians will not lapse back into militarism” after the war. As of now, the second negotiator added, Trump’s envoys do not see a way to do business with Russia without first achieving at least a partial cease-fire in Ukraine. But Coale’s strategy offers a possible work-around. The release of Russian political prisoners could give the U.S. a reason to ease sanctions, creating space for the financial transactions that Trump would like to pursue with the Russians. In Coale’s view, such deals could help bring the Ukraine war closer to a cease-fire by easing tensions between Russia and the West. “Economic ties usually result in normality,” he told me. C oale’s proposal emerged from a meeting he had this spring with a Russian dissident, Dmitry Muratov, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his decades of journalism and human-rights activism. The newspaper that Muratov co-founded and edited for many years, Novaya Gazeta , was forced to shut down soon after Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. Since then, Muratov has devoted most of his time to speaking out against the war and trying to free the Russian activists imprisoned for opposing it. Over the past year, he has closely followed reports of Coale’s work in Belarus, which I have written about at length . Coale and other U.S. diplomats have secured the release of about 500 political prisoners in Belarus, including a few American citizens. At the end of last year, Muratov asked me for an introduction to Coale. The dissident wanted to see whether Trump’s envoy could make the same appeals to the Kremlin as he had in Minsk. The release of prisoners, Muratov argued, has long been a part of American diplomacy in Moscow. At summits with Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, President Ronald Reagan or his envoys would often present the Soviets with lists of imprisoned dissidents and ask for their release. Gorbachev routinely obliged, creating a humanitarian dimension to his broader efforts to ease tensions with the Americans and reduce the risk of nuclear war. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, in 1991, Gorbachev and Muratov co-founded Novaya Gazeta and, over the years, it became Russia’s leading source of investigative reporting about the Kremlin’s abuses of power. Several of its journalists, including the legendary war reporter Anna Politkovskaya, have been murdered for their work. Before his death, in August 2022, at the age of 91, Gorbachev gave Muratov some of his possessions as keepsakes, including a commemorative medallion that Reagan gave to the Soviet leader at one of their summits. In May, Muratov brought the medallion to Washington and presented it to Coale as a token of admiration for his efforts in Belarus. Over plates of sushi at Ned’s Club, a members’ club popular among the political cognoscente, he told Trump’s envoy about the history of prisoner releases during the Cold War and the urgent need to revive this practice between the U.S. and Russia. Muratov brought photos of several of the dissidents whom Russia had jailed for their opposition to the war, and he told Coale their stories. He brought up the poet and theater director Evgenia Berkovich, who had picketed against the war in 2022. A Russian military court later sentenced her and her friend, the playwright Svetlana Petriychuk, to six years in prison on terrorism charges, part of a Kremlin campaign to criminalize any opposition to the war. Hundreds of people have been jailed in Russia for such offenses, some given years of incarceration for deeds as trivial as questioning the war in a comment on social media. Coale, for his part, described to Muratov the joy he felt the first time he managed to free a group of prisoners in Belarus last year. The experience gave the lawyer a new sense of purpose, he said, and he agreed to try a similar approach with the Russians. Soon after the meeting, Coale raised the idea with Trump, who gave his consent to try it, Coale told me. Yesterday, the White House nominated Coale to serve as the special presidential envoy for hostage affairs, with the rank of ambassador, a role that will require Senate confirmation. Asked to comment on his mission, a White House official said: “The President and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done.” Coale plans to coordinate his efforts with Steve Witkoff, who serves as Trump’s main point of contact with the Russians. A billionaire real-estate developer with no formal diplomatic experience, Witkoff has met with Putin at least seven times since the start of the war in Ukraine. During his most recent visit to the Kremlin, on September 5, the Russian leader expressed his gratitude to Witkoff and Kushner for their attempts to negotiate a peace deal. “I’d like to tell you that we find it comfortable to work with you, and, of course, we have a very high level of trust during this work,” Putin told the two Americans, according to footage of the meeting published on the Kremlin website. In response, Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing an American teacher, Bob Gilman, who had been jailed in Russia since 2022. Their conversation then shifted to the war in Ukraine. Kushner and Witkoff planned to fly from Moscow to Kyiv via Poland the next day, according to two people familiar with their travel arrangements. Neither of the American envoys had visited Ukraine during the war. As part of their preparations, Putin said, the Americans had requested a three-day cease-fire to allow the trip to proceed safely, and the Russians had given their consent. “I issued the respective order,” Putin said, adding that, since midnight that day, no strikes had been carried out on Kyiv. This appears to have been a lie. That morning, a Russian drone struck the territory of Kyiv’s main airport, in the city of Boryspil, where Witkoff and Kushner had been due to land the following day, according to the two people familiar with their travel plans. One of them, a Ukrainian official, showed me surveillance footage of the strike and photos of the crater it left near the runway. After the attack—which took place at 9:12 a.m. on September 5, while Kushner and Witkoff were flying to Moscow—the Americans changed their plans for the next day and traveled to Kyiv from Poland by train, the two people familiar with their trip told me. [ Read: Putin is slipping into delusion ] (The drone strike on Boryspil and its consequences have not been previously reported. A U.S. official familiar with the trip denied that Kushner and Witkoff changed their plans because of the airport attack but said that, in general, their travel arrangements often shift on short notice.) When informed of their need to reach Kyiv by train, the Ukrainian railway company scrambled to prepare a luxury cabin for the U.S. delegation, complete with a spread of Tatar cuisine from Crimea and a little sign on the dining table that said Peace arrives on time . A fter arriving in Kyiv, Kushner and Witkoff met for several hours with Zelensky and his team of negotiators. Two of them later told me that the talks focused on a variety of ways to achieve a limited cease-fire, which could be expanded into a broader peace deal to end the war in stages. “Their whole message right now is to shrink the conflict, in any way, from any direction,” one of the negotiators said of the Americans. Next month, he said, they aim to organize a gathering of envoys from the U.S., Russia, and Ukraine, most likely in Abu Dhabi, to discuss a limited cease-fire. It could oblige each side not to strike the other’s energy infrastructure, including power plants, oil refineries, and similar targets. A separate deal, mediated with help from the government of Egypt, would call for Russia and Ukraine not to strike one another’s cargo ships in the Black Sea, particularly those carrying grain to markets in the Middle East and Africa, the negotiators told me. The Americans have been keen to arrange a meeting with Trump, Putin, and Zelensky as soon as possible. On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. had invited Putin to the G20 summit to be held in December, at Trump’s golf club in Miami, where Trump could also try to bring Zelensky to the table. Putin has yet to accept the invitation. Regardless of the venue and format, Zelensky would be eager to participate in such a summit, one of his close aides told me: “He still has this idea that he can look Putin in the eyes and figure this out.” Putin has shown no such inclination. Although he seemed happy to host Kushner and Witkoff at the Kremlin this month, Russian attacks on Kyiv and other cities have grown deadlier and more frequent in recent weeks. For the first time since the start of the war, Russia has begun launching regular daytime strikes against the Ukrainian capital, killing or wounding scores of civilians, forcing businesses to close and schools to hold classes in bomb shelters. Two days before Kushner and Witkoff arrived in Kyiv, a Russian drone slammed into the headquarters of Ukraine’s main intelligence agency and exploded inside the office of its director. He survived the strike, but the Ukrainians saw it as a major escalation and a sign of Russia’s plans for the next few months. None of the handful of officials in Zelensky’s administration who spoke with me for this article expected Putin to engage in any serious peace talks until the spring at the earliest. “He has been stockpiling missiles for a reason, and he intends to use them this winter,” one of them told me. Given that lack of will on the Russian side, the flurry of peace talks initiated by Trump’s envoys in recent weeks has felt like a waste of time to some of the participants. As one of them described it to me the other day, “It almost feels like we’re all just dancing around Putin, offering him this and that, whatever we can think of, but he’s not moving.” C oale’s plan would seek to break that impasse. The issue of political prisoners, once introduced into the dialogue between the U.S. and Russia, would give Putin an easy way to demonstrate goodwill and create fresh signs of diplomatic progress with the Americans while continuing to terrorize Ukraine. Last month’s release of Gilman, the American teacher, serves as a case in point, and Coale told me that he has already gathered a list of other Americans held in Russian prisons. A separate list, compiled with help from Muratov, will include dissidents, journalists, and others incarcerated for their opposition to the war. Trade and business talks would run parallel to these discussions, and one business deal has already demonstrated how they could work, expanding the points of contact between the U.S. and Russia beyond the peace talks in Ukraine, Coale told me. Last Tuesday, Trump announced on Truth Social that the U.S. was working on “a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” adding that it would be “very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.” That deal resulted in large part from Coale’s work. In response to the release of political prisoners, the U.S. lifted some of its sanctions on that country’s regime to allow the deal to proceed. The discussions also involve Russia, Coale explained. European countries have not agreed to ease their own sanctions on Belarus, and they have refused to allow the transport of potash from Belarus across their territory. That means it would most likely need to move eastward through Russia before reaching international markets, making the Kremlin a party to the deal. [ Read: The irreversible change in Belarus ] “If the West is buying potash, then they’ve got to deal with the Russians and the Belarusians. So you’re sitting down at a table, and you’re haggling over price or finding the routes to get it out,” Coale told me. “When people talk, it’s a good thing. Even if they’re talking about potash, it may go into having the countries, as I say, going back to the family of nations with the rest of the world.” Coale said his strategy would not abandon Ukraine, but it would seek to strengthen ties between the U.S. and Russia, encouraging Putin to end the war as part of a broader agenda of business and trade with the West. By switching from the stick of sanctions to the carrot of mutual profits, this plan follows a lesson Coale learned last year from Putin’s closest ally, the Belarusian dictator Lukashenko. “In the name of peace, maybe you’ve got to be a little cunning and make some concessions,” Lukashenko told me last August, describing the advice he gave Coale for dealing with the Kremlin. “Even if you can’t make sense of Putin, treat him like a human being.” As the U.S. began easing sanctions on Belarus last year, Lukashenko helped the Americans arrange a summit with Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, where Trump greeted the Russian leader on a red carpet. Their talks did not result in any breakthrough in the efforts to end the war in Ukraine. On the contrary, Russia only intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s power plants, apartment blocks, and other civilian targets. But the Alaska summit did ease the diplomatic isolation of Ukraine’s main adversaries. On his flight to Anchorage aboard Air Force One, Trump called Lukashenko to thank him for releasing political prisoners and, in a post on social media, referred to the despot as a “Highly Respected President.” Ever since, Coale has continued working with Lukashenko to win the release of prisoners and negotiate business deals. His approach has alarmed many diplomats in Europe, who have called on the U.S. to maintain its sanctions pressure on Belarus and Russia. The leader of the democratic opposition in Belarus, Svetlana Tikhanovskaya, told me last week that the exchange of prisoners for sanctions relief will only encourage the regimes in Russia and Belarus to take more prisoners. “This trade in human beings costs them nothing,” she said during her visit to New York for the UN General Assembly. “They can always arrest more people, while the West loses its leverage over these regimes by lifting sanctions and making deals.” Tikhanovskaya’s own husband, a prominent blogger in Belarus who tried to run for president against the country’s dictator in 2020, was freed from prison last year in a release that Coale negotiated with the regime. When I pointed out the contradiction in Tikhanovskaya’s stance, she struggled for a moment to explain it. Her family, which now lives in exile, had been reunited thanks to the Trump administration’s strategy of swapping economic deals for foreign detainees. Yet she now argues that the families of other political prisoners should not benefit from such trades. “I know it seems unfair,” she said finally. “But if we do this, in Russia or in Belarus, those regimes will take more hostages, and their families will go through the same horrors that we did.” Muratov’s stance on this dilemma bears an even greater irony. He lives in Moscow, and the prominence bestowed on him by the Nobel Peace Prize would make him a valuable prisoner for the Kremlin to trade away. Russian authorities recently began investigating his taxes, which could give the Kremlin an easy excuse to put Muratov in jail and offer him up to the Americans in exchange for sanctions relief. But the dissident does not seem deterred by that risk. If Coale’s campaign frees the innocent people already jailed in Russia for speaking out against the war, Muratov told me, it will have been worth it for them and their families, even if the story ends with him in a prison cell. Ashley Parker contributed reporting to this article.

articles.title: Báo Xây dựng tổ chức tọa đàm “Quy định mới trong quản lý xe hợp đồng”
articles.text:
Cùng với sự phát triển của thị trường vận tải, xe hợp đồng đã đáp ứng nhu cầu đi lại linh hoạt, đa dạng của người dân.
Tuy nhiên, bên cạnh những doanh nghiệp chấp hành nghiêm các quy định, thực tế vẫn còn tình trạng một số xe hợp đồng hoạt động chưa đúng bản chất, đón, trả khách tùy tiện, hình thành các điểm giao dịch không đúng quy định, ảnh hưởng đến trật tự vận tải và môi trường cạnh tranh giữa các loại hình kinh doanh.
Trước yêu cầu đó, Chính phủ đã ban hành các Nghị định số 336/2025/NĐ-CP, 218/2026/NĐ-CP và 238/2026/NĐ-CP, trong đó có những quy định nhằm tiếp tục hoàn thiện khuôn khổ pháp lý, tăng cường quản lý hoạt động vận tải hành khách theo hợp đồng.
Các quy định mới không chỉ đặt ra yêu cầu đối với doanh nghiệp, lái xe mà còn mở ra những phương thức quản lý, giám sát gắn với ứng dụng công nghệ và dữ liệu.
Nhằm tăng cường truyền thông chính sách, nâng cao ý thức tuân thủ pháp luật, nâng cao chất lượng dịch vụ vận tải hành khách và bảo đảm trật tự, an toàn giao thông, Báo Xây dựng tổ chức tọa đàm trường quay “Quy định mới trong quản lý xe hợp đồng”.
Tọa đàm diễn ra lúc 8h30 ngày 30/9/2026, được phát trực tuyến trên các nền tảng mạng xã hội của Báo Xây dựng và tường thuật trực tiếp trên Báo điện tử Xây dựng.
Khách mời tham gia tọa đàm
1. Thượng tá Nguyễn Hồng Long, Phó Trưởng phòng Hướng dẫn tuyên truyền, điều tra, giải quyết tai nạn giao thông, Cục Cảnh sát giao thông.
2. Ông Đỗ Quốc Phong, Phó Trưởng phòng Quản lý vận tải, Cục Đường bộ Việt Nam.
3. Ông Nguyễn Công Hùng, Phó Chủ tịch Hiệp hội Vận tải ô tô Việt Nam.

articles.title: The Art of Dealing With Trump
articles.text: T he best metaphor for trade negotiations may be trying to arrange a marriage. Countries come to the table with friendly intentions, hoping to form a partnership. The pressure is to make a deal, not to block one, and if they don’t succeed, that is a cause for sorrow, not anger. Donald Trump has changed all of that. He has turned trade deals from negotiations about marriage to threats of divorce. Before Trump, the Western consensus had long been that free trade made individual countries richer overall, and the world richer too. Trump does not believe that. More importantly, his trade negotiations aren’t only, or even mostly, about trade. They are about domestic politics and geopolitics, and, above all, they are about staging a drama in which he, and America, wins. Trump is trying to turn trade from a win-win relationship to a battle for dominance over adversaries and a protection racket for friends. This is trade policy as per Roald Dahl’s Matilda rather than Adam Smith. The organizing principle for this MAGA administration is that countries need to pay for the right to sell things to the United States. They can pay quite literally, through tariffs. They can pay by pledging investments in the U.S. And they can pay with actions that have no connection to trade but that the White House wants. Most of America’s allies have simply capitulated—accepting harmful and unjust tariffs or offering other forms of tribute. [ Read: Why Trump has it out for Canada ] My experience as Canada’s international trade minister and foreign minister during the first Trump administration suggests another possible strategy. A decade ago, Trump threatened to tear up the North American Free Trade Agreement and destroy Canada’s most important trade relationship. Canada was gobsmacked, but we were also prepared. In the summer of 2016, our ambassador began to warn us that Trump might win. So I asked our outstanding trade officials to prepare a memo outlining what we should do if a victorious Trump carried through on his campaign-trail attacks on NAFTA. We called it the “in emergency, break glass” briefing note. In the days after the election, that homework paid off. Canada was angry, but we also stayed calm. We met Trump and his team at the table, looked for things we could agree about, and held firm to our red lines. Throughout two years of negotiation, Trump and his minions insulted and demeaned Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and me, calling me a “nasty woman” who “hates America.” In 2018, he imposed illegal and unjustified tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. Canada then did something that much of the world has forgotten how to do: We fought back, with dollar-for-dollar reciprocal tariffs. Because ultimately, the only thing that works with this president is strength. During our years of negotiating, we developed a three-part playbook for handling the Trump administration. It eventually got us to a great deal, and it can help America’s allies deal with the White House today. First: Look for areas where you agree and can work together. Second, apply the doughnut strategy: Yes, the president is important, but he is just one figure in the middle of a big country. Be sure to talk with Americans in the rest of the doughnut, not just in the Oval Office in the middle. Third, and most important: Do not capitulate. D uring the NAFTA negotiations , we shuttled back and forth to Washington more than a dozen times. The talks were high drama. Sometimes the Americans yelled at us; at other times, they graciously served us snacks, including Hershey’s Kisses with packaging signed by Donald Trump. As we waited in the White House for a bilateral meeting between the president and the prime minister, a smiling, jocular Gary Cohn, a senior economic aide to Trump at the time, once told me: “You’re definitely going to get screwed. The only question is whether you get screwed with a kiss.” Occasionally, I would take refuge in the ladies’ washroom—generally a safe space, because there were usually no women on the U.S. side of the table. Once, at a particularly dire moment, I got down on my knees there and prayed. Holding your ground when Trump demands that you buckle is not easy. Political rivals accused our team of “Napping on NAFTA” and said we should accept more of Trump’s proposals. In response, I said then what I believe now: “Capitulation is not a negotiating strategy.” This article has been adapted from Chrystia Freeland’s new book, Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider’s View of Dealing With a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People . That doesn’t preclude finding areas of agreement. Trump lies so much about trade that it can be hard to recognize when he has a point. But the fact is that the old NAFTA, and the free-trade consensus it represented, really did have problems. For example, Trump was right that the low wages paid to Mexican auto workers undermined American workers, especially in the states that had gotten him elected in 2016. We had dealt with similar concerns when negotiating an earlier trade deal between Canada and the European Union: European socialists, much like American right-wing populists, wanted deals that supported high wages for workers and that protected national sovereignty against multinational corporations. I agreed. And that is one reason we were able to make a deal with Donald Trump. The Americans demanded that a specific quota of U.S.-made parts be included in a NAFTA-compliant car. We made a counterproposal: A certain percentage of the car had to be manufactured by workers making at least $16 an hour. This would become one of the smartest features of the new NAFTA, designed to protect the jobs that had been outsourced since the original deal while disarming American efforts to kill the Canadian auto industry. But for Trump, getting a good deal isn’t really the point. In 2018, the United States levied illegal and unjustified tariffs against Canadian steel and aluminum, claiming that our exports were a threat to U.S. national security. I pushed for retaliation, and Prime Minister Trudeau agreed. We weren’t a security threat to America; to suggest that we were was insulting. We were responding more in sorrow than in anger. But this was a big move, the largest trade retaliation Canada had imposed since the second world war. We targeted goods that would cause maximum political pain in the United States and do little damage in Canada: ketchup and jam made in Pennsylvania and Ohio, to put pressure on the president’s Rust Belt constituency; bourbon and playing cards, to make an impact in Kentucky, home to Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and the U.S. ambassador to Canada, Kelly Craft; and cheese and yogurt to pressure House Speaker Paul Ryan of Wisconsin. [ Read: Europe and Canada are like the kids in an ugly divorce ] Canada didn’t start this fight. We were simply responding, dollar for dollar, to the tariffs the U.S. had imposed on our steel and aluminum. We coordinated with Mexico and the EU to maximize our impact, and we left room for negotiation by waiting a month after U.S. tariffs went into force before imposing our own. When we announced our retaliatory action, I told Canadians that I had spoken with Robert Lighthizer, the U.S. trade representative, six times in the previous week and that Canada was willing to talk any place, any time. The mere declaration that we were going to retaliate infuriated President Trump. He started bullying Canada and Canadian leaders publicly and privately. Just as we were getting ready to unveil our final tariff list, Trump made a personal phone call to Trudeau, in which he threatened dire consequences, including destroying the Canadian auto industry, if we went through with our plan. He told Trudeau that I was a “nasty woman” who had spoken critically about him to other world leaders. Peter Navarro, the White House’s trade adviser, hastily dismissed the impact of retaliatory tariffs as little more than a “rounding error” for the U.S. economy, but Trump’s intemperance betrayed greater anxiety. Many Canadian business leaders were anxious about an all-out trade war with the United States, and at least one of my cabinet colleagues, the finance minister, argued that we should postpone our trade action beyond the one-month grace period we had already extended and just keep talking. I understood the fear. A trade fight with the United States would be more painful for us than for the Americans, as the $16.6 billion in goods targeted by the tariffs was 0.06 percent of the U.S. GDP, but 0.74 percent of ours. We also had more at stake: Trade accounts for about 65 percent of the Canadian economy, and more than 70 percent of our exports were to the United States in 2018. Trade is about 25 percent of the U.S. economy, and 18 percent of U.S. exports were to Canada in 2018. But I was absolutely certain that we needed to fight back, and I was equally confident that if we did so, we would succeed. Trump is a textbook bully. For him, weakness is a provocation. But when he is met with strength, he finds a way to make a deal. Trump doesn’t always chicken out, per the TACO meme. Just ask Nicolás Maduro. But he does find ways to change course when the other side keeps its nerve, as the dictators in Beijing and Tehran—and the Democrats in Minneapolis—have shown. The economic facts had always been on our side. Trade between Canada and the United States was balanced, mutually beneficial, and made both of our countries more secure. Our countries had been building things together since Henry Ford manufactured the first Model T, and Canada was a secure and reliable supplier of oil and electricity to the United States. The value of this partnership should have been enough to secure a deal—and it had been, for decades. But with this president, facts alone don’t matter, and a win-win outcome is a last resort. We had to prove to him that he couldn’t bully Canada, and that trade with Canada was actually in America’s national interest. Only by demonstrating painful consequences could we get back to a reciprocal relationship with our neighbor. We also knew that we needed to talk with people other than Trump. Among the Republican allies we courted, starting in 2017, was Paul Ryan, the speaker of the House, whose home state of Wisconsin exported nearly $7 billion a year to Canada. “I just like trade,” Ryan told me, saying that among partners, “Canada is the one that’s fair and balanced.” I met with Arizona Senator John McCain, who warned me that some of the tariff proposals, including those involving Canada, were “nuts, crazy, insane.” But he said that he would “lay down on the tracks” to oppose that approach and that “there’s enough Republicans who are against it.” Fewer than four weeks after our retaliatory tariffs went into effect, in July 2018, a business coalition supported by farm-state political leaders on both sides of the aisle launched a multimillion-dollar campaign called “Tariffs Hurt the Heartland.” They held 15 town halls across the Midwest and carried out three aggressive ad campaigns, including one called “Rounding Error” and one titled simply “Tariffs Are a Tax.” This political pressure on Trump, including from his own supporters, kept the talks on track through difficult weeks. It also enraged the president. But ultimately, and quite rightly, the people whose views most mattered to the administration were Americans themselves. They were the lobbyists who really counted. And that is why retaliation, together with the doughnut strategy, was so important. In arguing that tariffs and counter-tariffs couldn’t really hurt the United States because international trade was relatively unimportant to the American economy, Navarro and like-minded economists made the same mistake that globalization advocates once made. They failed to account for the pain their policy would cause specific people and specific communities. Tariffs might be a “rounding error” in aggregate, but for some people and some places, they were devastating. Ground zero for tariff pain was Iowa, a farm state where one in five jobs depended on trade. By May, coordinated retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada and other countries hurt by the U.S. had cost the state’s farmers, particularly pork and soybean producers, nearly $1.5 billion in lost export revenue. That came out to roughly $17,000 per farm. The Tariffs Hurt the Heartland campaign created an interactive map, populated with heart-wrenching stories from midwesterners. W hen President Trump took office for his second term last year, he was met with a wave of capitulation. Many American CEOs, lawyers, and university presidents bowed their heads to avoid his wrath. America’s international allies largely surrendered too—knuckling under in response to tariffs, appeasing the president at the first NATO summit, and responding to insults and ridicule during White House visits with sycophancy and fixed smiles. But America’s allies have also shown that they can stand Trump down. When Trump threatened to seize Greenland in January 2026, the EU did not give in. And Greenland remains part of the Kingdom of Denmark, following some clever diplomacy by Copenhagen, which succeeded in reaffirming its sovereignty without reigniting the war of words. [ Read: America’s allies are no longer waiting for Trump to leave ] Many of us in allied countries feel so angry, so frightened, and so betrayed right now that we easily forget how much we have prospered, together, during the American century. Pax Americana has not always been benign, of course, and living with a hegemon is often uncomfortable. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, Justin’s father, brilliantly compared sharing a border with the United States to sleeping next to an elephant: Even if the elephant is gracious and well disposed toward you, you never sleep altogether easily. A lot has changed since 2018, but I still believe two things that I believed then—that America can be a force for good in the world, and that we need to be frank with our American friends about how profoundly they are losing our trust. The official public obsequiousness that is the love language of the Oval Office, and which America is hearing from too much of the world, masks a disenchantment that is hardening into contempt. Rather than containing the president, his appeasers have enabled him. America’s allies must speak out, and they must do so together. Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is showing America’s other friends that when you stand up to a bully, you can rally your country behind you. That approach worked in 2018, and it can work today. And, ultimately, it is in America’s best interest too. By refusing to submit, we can help Americans remember that the most effective way to treat their allies—and not just authoritarian tyrants—is with partnership, not punishment. If America can relearn that lesson, which the postwar generation first taught, it will be a win-win outcome for democrats and democracies everywhere. This article has been adapted from Chrystia Freeland’s new book, Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider’s View of Dealing With a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People .

articles.title: AFC nói gì khi Việt Nam gục ngã trước Thái Lan?
articles.text:
TPO - Trang chủ Liên đoàn Bóng đá châu Á gọi bàn thắng mở tỷ số của Sarach là pha sút xa tuyệt vời. Trong khi đó, Việt Nam tạo ra nhiều cơ hội nhưng không tận dụng được.
Ảnh: Hữu Phạm.
"Voi chiến đã chấm dứt chuỗi 27 trận bất bại của Việt Nam và giành vé vào chung kết FIFA ASEAN Cup sớm một lượt đấu. Trước khi 2 đội gặp nhau, Việt Nam có phong độ rất tốt với chuỗi bất bại kéo dài 2 năm. Hành trình tuyệt vời của thầy trò HLV Kim đã kết thúc dưới tay đối thủ truyền kiếp Thái Lan", AFC bình luận.
"Bàn thắng tuyệt vời của Sarach mở đầu cho chiến thắng của Thái Lan. Chỉ sau 10 phút, bóng đến chân đội trưởng Thái Lan và anh tung ra cú sút xa đẹp mắt từ khoảng cách 25m, đánh bại hoàn toàn Patrik Lê Giang. Đó là bàn thắng thứ 9 trong 97 trận ra sân của Sarach cho Thái Lan", AFC viết tiếp.
Trang chủ LĐBĐ châu Á nhận định Việt Nam gặp may khi cú sút phạt ngoạn mục tiếp theo của Sarach đưa bóng dội cột. Việt Nam đã gặp khó khăn trong suốt hiệp 1 để đáp trả "Voi chiến". "Sang hiệp 2, Việt Nam có cơ hội của Hoàng Đức và Đình Bắc nhưng đều bỏ lỡ. Sau đó, Patrik Lê Giang cứu thua xuất thần để cản phá pha dứt điểm của Peeradol ở phút cuối", AFC nhấn mạnh.
HLV Kim bất lực ở trận này. Ảnh: Hữu Phạm.
"Thái Lan sẽ xoay vòng đội hình ở trận đấu cuối, trong khi Việt Nam cần giành một điểm trước Pakistan để bước vào trận tranh hạng ba", AFC kết luận.
Thầy trò HLV Anthony Hudson đã chơi một trận thực dụng, ưu tiên phòng ngự chắc chắn và biết cách tận dụng cơ hội để kết liễu Việt Nam. "Các chiến binh sao vàng" cầm bóng nhiều hơn, tạo ra nhiều tình huống tấn công có nét hơn hẳn nhưng khâu dứt điểm cuối cùng của Hoàng Đức, Đình Bắc và các tiền đạo Việt Nam không hoàn hảo ở trận này.
Đến khi Tài Lộc đánh bại thủ môn của Thái Lan và đưa bóng vào khung thành, pha lập công bị hủy vì lỗi việt vị. Đây là trận thua xứng đáng của Việt Nam khi chúng ta không tận dụng được cơ hội tốt như Thái Lan. Hệ thống phòng ngự của nhà ĐKVĐ ASEAN Cup cũng lộ ra rất nhiều vấn đề.
Xem FIFA ASEAN CUP 2026 trực tiếp & trọn vẹn trên FPT Play, TV360 và MyTV.

articles.title: Báo Indonesia: Hàng công Việt Nam thiếu đột biến vì vắng Xuân Son
articles.text:
Trong bài tường thuật trận đấu, CNN Indonesia nhận định trận thua 0-2 trước Thái Lan tại lượt trận thứ hai bảng B - FIFA ASEAN Cup 2026 không chỉ khiến Việt Nam đánh mất tấm vé vào chung kết, mà còn cho thấy những hạn chế trên mặt trận tấn công của các học trò HLV Kim Sang-sik ở giải này.
Một trong những tâm điểm đáng chú ý nhất, theo tờ báo Indonesia, là sự thiếu vắng của Xuân Son sau khi tiền đạo này gặp chấn thương từ giữa trận thắng Philippines và phải chia tay giải đấu. “Việc không có Nguyễn Xuân Son khiến tuyến đầu của Việt Nam thiếu hẳn khả năng tạo bất ngờ”, tờ CNN Indonesia nhận định.
Thực tế, Việt Nam bước vào trận đấu với Thái Lan sau khi chỉ ghi được một bàn trong chiến thắng tối thiểu trước Philippines. Trong khi đó, Thái Lan đã có màn khởi đầu tưng bừng với chiến thắng 4-0 trước Pakistan và còn giữ được tiền vệ ngôi sao Chanathip trên ghế dự bị để giữ sức cho trận gặp Việt Nam.
Sự chênh lệch ấy tiếp tục được thể hiện trên sân Si Jalak Harupat khi Việt Nam không thể tìm thấy phương án đủ sắc bén để xuyên thủng hàng phòng ngự Thái Lan. Người thay thế Xuân Son là Tài Lộc tuy đã rất cố gắng nhưng không thể khỏa lấp được khoảng trống mà ngôi sao mang áo số 12 để lại.
Xuân Son không chỉ đơn thuần là một trung phong có khả năng ghi bàn. Sự hiện diện của Vua phá lưới ASEAN Hyundai Cup còn tạo ra một điểm đến rõ ràng cho những đường chuyền trực diện, đồng thời buộc hàng thủ đối phương phải dành thêm người để theo kèm. Khi không có anh, Việt Nam thiếu một mũi nhọn đủ sức kéo giãn hệ thống phòng ngự Thái Lan và mở ra khoảng trống cho các vệ tinh.
Điều đó càng trở nên rõ ràng trước một Thái Lan chơi rất tỉnh táo. Đội bóng xứ Chùa Vàng không cần phòng ngự quá sâu hay mạo hiểm để bảo vệ khung thành. “Với một bộ khung giàu kinh nghiệm, Thái Lan duy trì được cự ly đội hình hợp lý, hạn chế không gian hoạt động của các cầu thủ tấn công Việt Nam và chờ đợi thời cơ phản công”, CNN Indonesia phân tích.
Nếu hàng công Việt Nam thiếu đột biến, hàng thủ Thái Lan lại cho thấy sự kiên nhẫn đáng kể. Các hậu vệ của đội bóng áo xanh không dễ dàng bị kéo ra khỏi vị trí, đồng thời xử lý khá bình tĩnh trước những pha phối hợp của đối thủ. Đây là khác biệt quan trọng giữa một hàng phòng ngự có tổ chức và một hàng phòng ngự chỉ đơn thuần chống đỡ sức ép.
Trước đó, Việt Nam từng đánh bại Thái Lan 2-0 ngay tại Bangkok ở trận chung kết lượt đi ASEAN Hyundai Cup 2026, trước khi hòa 2-2 ở lượt về tại Mỹ Đình để bảo vệ chức vô địch. Tuy nhiên, lần tái đấu này cho thấy Thái Lan đã chuẩn bị một cách tiếp cận khác, đặc biệt trong khả năng kiểm soát những mũi tấn công chủ lực của Việt Nam.
“Sau giờ nghỉ giữa hiệp, Việt Nam giành lại quyền kiểm soát trận đấu. Sự xuất hiện của Đỗ Hoàng Hên, Williams Minh Hoàng và Nguyễn Hoàng Đức đã gia tăng sức mạnh tấn công cho Việt Nam. Nhưng đội bóng của HLV Kim Sang-sik vẫn không thể tìm ra giải pháp phá vỡ hàng phòng ngự Thái Lan”, CNN Indonesia bình luận.
Khi dồn toàn lực tấn công mà không thể ghi bàn, việc Việt Nam nhận bàn thua thứ hai ở phút 90+3 là kết cục không quá bất ngờ. Dẫu vậy, thất bại của Các chiến binh Sao vàng cũng được giới mộ điệu Indonesia nhìn nhận dưới một lăng kính khá tôn trọng.
Nhiều ý kiến trên các diễn đàn bóng đá Indonesia cho rằng, trận này Việt Nam thua bởi Thái Lan chơi quá hay. “Dù có nhiều cầu thủ lớn tuổi, lối chơi của Thái Lan vẫn rất xuất sắc, với những đường ban bật chính xác và dứt điểm hoàn hảo”, một số CĐV trong diễn đàn Sepakbola Indonesia Fansbook đánh giá. Một số khác thậm chí còn đi xa hơn khi cho rằng, cứ đá như thế này, Thái Lan xứng đáng là đội bóng số một Đông Nam Á.

articles.title: VEC đề xuất tham gia đầu tư mở rộng hai tuyến cao tốc lớn
articles.text:
Tổng công ty Đầu tư phát triển đường cao tốc Việt Nam (VEC) vừa có văn bản gửi Bộ Xây dựng, đề xuất đầu tư mở rộng tuyến cao tốc Bắc - Nam phía Đông và một số tuyến cao tốc khác theo phương thức đối tác công - tư (PPP).
Căn cứ danh mục 29 dự án đường bộ cao tốc ưu tiên xúc tiến, kêu gọi đầu tư theo phương thức PPP giai đoạn 2026-2030, VEC kiến nghị Bộ Xây dựng xem xét giao doanh nghiệp nghiên cứu, lập hồ sơ đề xuất dự án mở rộng tuyến cao tốc Bắc - Nam phía Đông, đoạn Mai Sơn - Cam Lộ hoặc đoạn từ Quảng Ngãi đến Dầu Giây.
VEC cũng đề xuất được lập hồ sơ đề xuất dự án mở rộng tuyến cao tốc Nội Bài - Hạ Long, đoạn Nội Bài - Bắc Ninh, với tổng chiều dài khoảng 30km, nhằm bảo đảm kết nối đồng bộ với dự án Vành đai 4 Vùng Thủ đô do VEC đang là nhà đầu tư.
Trường hợp được Bộ Xây dựng chấp thuận, VEC cam kết chủ động bố trí kinh phí từ nguồn vốn sản xuất, kinh doanh của doanh nghiệp để thực hiện công tác chuẩn bị đầu tư; tổ chức lập, hoàn thiện hồ sơ và trình cấp có thẩm quyền xem xét, thẩm định, quyết định theo quy định của pháp luật.
Khẳng định năng lực trong đầu tư, quản lý và vận hành đường cao tốc, VEC cho biết đã và đang đầu tư nhiều dự án như: Cầu Giẽ - Ninh Bình (dài 50km); Nội Bài - Lào Cai (dài 245km); TP.HCM - Long Thành - Dầu Giây (dài 55km); Đà Nẵng - Quảng Ngãi (dài gần 140km); Bến Lức - Long Thành (dài 58km); Dự án thành phần 3 thuộc tuyến Vành đai 4 Vùng Thủ đô Hà Nội (dài 113km).
Hiện nay, VEC và các đơn vị thành viên đang quản lý, khai thác khoảng 1.120km đường bộ trên phạm vi cả nước. Trong đó, khoảng 520km thuộc 5 tuyến đường bộ cao tốc do VEC làm chủ đầu tư và gần 600km do Bộ Xây dựng cùng các địa phương đầu tư.
Theo báo cáo tài chính đến ngày 31/12/2025, vốn chủ sở hữu của VEC khoảng 45.443 tỷ đồng, hệ số nợ/vốn chủ sở hữu là 1,09. VEC cho rằng với quy mô vốn chủ sở hữu hiện có, doanh nghiệp có khả năng huy động vốn, đáp ứng nhu cầu đầu tư mở rộng cao tốc Bắc - Nam phía Đông.
